schema_note: Third profile authored with the five fields from docs/reference/profile-sufficiency.md (operations, domain, failures, swap_axis, vocabulary), after 1.5 and 6.1. `swap_axis` is sourced here by the same instrument 6.1 produced -- read the standard's own scope statement -- but it inverted: OpenLineage's scope statement names the transport as configurable, which makes protocol the *cosmetic* axis and sends the real one somewhere else. That refinement is recorded in the sufficiency note. `standards` is deliberately empty; see gaps.

definition.text: Lineage at this card is the record of which run consumed which inputs and produced which outputs, kept as an event stream about a job while it executes rather than as a property of a stored artifact. The framework states its own subject -- "OpenLineage is an open framework for data lineage collection and analysis. At its core is an extensible specification that systems can use to interoperate with lineage metadata." -- and what it records: "OpenLineage is an Open Standard for lineage metadata collection designed to record metadata for a job in execution." The noun set is three entities plus an extension point: "The standard defines a generic model of dataset, job, and run entities uniquely identified using consistent naming strategies. The core model is highly extensible via facets."

evidence.quote: OpenLineage is an open framework for data lineage collection and analysis. At its core is an extensible specification that systems can use to interoperate with lineage metadata.
OpenLineage is an Open Standard for lineage metadata collection designed to record metadata for a job in execution.
The standard defines a generic model of dataset, job, and run entities uniquely identified using consistent naming strategies. The core model is highly extensible via facets.

operations.text: The operation set is an event stream with a stated minimum rather than a list of verbs -- "**Run Event**: an event describing an observed state of a job run. Sending at least a START event and a COMPLETE/FAIL/ABORT event is required. Additional events are optional." The order half of the field, which docs/reference/profile-sufficiency.md required, is answerable here and is a *partial* order rather than a sequence. Three states close a run: "Unless specified otherwise, we assume events describing a single run are accumulative and COMPLETE, ABORT and FAIL are terminal events. Sending any of terminal events means no other events related to this run will be emitted." One state is explicitly outside the ordering: "Additionally, we allow OTHER to be sent anytime before the terminal states, also before START." So what a conformance check can assert is that START precedes any terminal event, that at most one terminal event occurs, and that nothing follows it -- but not a fixed sequence, because RUNNING may repeat and OTHER may arrive before START. This is the second measured shape of the order question: card 6.1 had one verb and no order at all, 3.3 had a strict lifecycle, and 6.3 has a partial order with a declared exemption.

evidence.quote: **Run Event**: an event describing an observed state of a job run. Sending at least a START event and a COMPLETE/FAIL/ABORT event is required. Additional events are optional.

Unless specified otherwise, we assume events describing a single run are accumulative and COMPLETE, ABORT and FAIL are terminal events. Sending any of terminal events means no other events related to this run will be emitted.
Additionally, we allow OTHER to be sent anytime before the terminal states, also before START.

domain.text: Three fields the card names have stated domains. The run state: "There are six run states currently defined in the OpenLineage spec: START to indicate the beginning of a Job RUNNING to provide additional information about a running Job COMPLETE to signify that execution of the Job has concluded ABORT to signify that the Job has been stopped abnormally FAIL to signify that the Job has failed OTHER to send additional metadata outside standard run cycle" Of those, "Unless specified otherwise, we assume events describing a single run are accumulative and COMPLETE, ABORT and FAIL are terminal events. Sending any of terminal events means no other events related to this run will be emitted." The run identifier: "**Run**: An instance of a running job with a start and completion (or failure) time. A run is identified by a globally unique ID relative to its job definition." And the write semantics of the extension point, which is a domain question a consumer gets wrong by default -- facets do not merge: "A facet is an atomic piece of metadata identified by its name. This means that emitting a new facet with the same name for the same entity replaces the previous facet instance for that entity entirely."

evidence.quote: There are six run states currently defined in the OpenLineage spec: START to indicate the beginning of a Job RUNNING to provide additional information about a running Job COMPLETE to signify that execution of the Job has concluded ABORT to signify that the Job has been stopped abnormally FAIL to signify that the Job has failed OTHER to send additional metadata outside standard run cycle

Unless specified otherwise, we assume events describing a single run are accumulative and COMPLETE, ABORT and FAIL are terminal events. Sending any of terminal events means no other events related to this run will be emitted.
**Run**: An instance of a running job with a start and completion (or failure) time. A run is identified by a globally unique ID relative to its job definition.

A facet is an atomic piece of metadata identified by its name. This means that emitting a new facet with the same name for the same entity replaces the previous facet instance for that entity entirely.

failures.text: Failure at this card is a run state rather than an error object, and the state set is closed: FAIL and ABORT are two of the six enumerated states, both terminal -- "Unless specified otherwise, we assume events describing a single run are accumulative and COMPLETE, ABORT and FAIL are terminal events. Sending any of terminal events means no other events related to this run will be emitted." The detail is carried in a facet rather than in the event's shape: "**errorMessage**: Captures the error message, programming language - and optionally stack trace - when a run fails." That is the whole of it. There is no typed failure for the act of *emitting* lineage -- nothing says what a producer does when the backend refuses an event, or whether an unemitted event is a failure of the run. Proposed, and the reason: this repo has built no adapter at this card, so what a path that has never run must return -- the half of this field added after card 3.3 -- cannot be answered from evidence here either. Fourth card, same answer; see gaps.

evidence.quote: Unless specified otherwise, we assume events describing a single run are accumulative and COMPLETE, ABORT and FAIL are terminal events. Sending any of terminal events means no other events related to this run will be emitted.
**errorMessage**: Captures the error message, programming language - and optionally stack trace - when a run fails.

vocabulary.text: This card grants the caller an *open-ended* vocabulary, which is different from every other card profiled so far and is the interesting fact about it. The unit is a facet -- "**Facet**: A piece of metadata attached to one of the entities defined above." -- and the step it applies at is the event: a facet is attached to one of the three core entities on a run event, not configured once at startup. Rather than a closed value list, the standard gives a collision rule -- "Custom facets must use a distinct prefix named after the project defining them to avoid collision with standard facets" -- and a shape: "Naming of custom facets should follow the pattern `{prefix}{name}{entity}Facet` PascalCased." There is even a route out of caller-space into the standard: "Custom facets can be promoted to the standard by including them in the spec." Proposed: this repo has not built an adapter at this card, so no mapping from its own `intent:` / `profile:` vocabulary onto a facet prefix has been chosen. That makes four cards -- 3.3, 1.5, 6.1, 6.3 -- where the standard supplies the words and nothing supplies the join.

evidence.quote: **Facet**: A piece of metadata attached to one of the entities defined above.
Custom facets must use a distinct prefix named after the project defining them to avoid collision with standard facets
Naming of custom facets should follow the pattern `{prefix}{name}{entity}Facet` PascalCased.
Custom facets can be promoted to the standard by including them in the spec.

swap_axis.text: What a second implementation must differ on for a swap at this card to be real. The scope statement is where card 6.1 found this answer, and here the same instrument gives the *negative* result, which is why it is worth stating: "OpenLineage defines the metadata for running jobs and their corresponding events. A configurable backend allows the user to choose what protocol to send the events to." The protocol is declared configurable, so swapping it is the intended, cheap substitution -- and therefore exactly the relabelling a swap test must not be satisfied by. The real axis is one field further in, and the standard declares it: "Jobs can have different processing types that define their lifecycle characteristics. The JobTypeJobFacet processingType field indicates the nature of the job:" A finite job and a continuous one are not two labels on one lifecycle. "BATCH jobs are finite jobs with a clear start and end point. They are expected to terminate naturally after completing their work." against "STREAMING jobs are continuous jobs that process data streams indefinitely with no natural completion point." -- and the standard tells a consumer outright that the difference changes what may be read back: "While START, COMPLETE, ABORT, or FAIL events can be emitted, they should not be relied upon as they might occur only occasionally when the streaming job is restarted" A second axis of the same kind sits beside it: "The eventCompleteness field in the emission pattern describes what information events contain:" where a snapshot event stands alone -- "Each event is self-contained for its time period" -- and an accumulative one does not. So a genuine adapter pair here is batch-with-terminal-event against streaming-with-periodic-snapshots, and a conformance check can read the difference off the event stream: whether waiting for a terminal event ever returns.

evidence.quote: OpenLineage defines the metadata for running jobs and their corresponding events. A configurable backend allows the user to choose what protocol to send the events to.
Jobs can have different processing types that define their lifecycle characteristics. The JobTypeJobFacet processingType field indicates the nature of the job:
BATCH jobs are finite jobs with a clear start and end point. They are expected to terminate naturally after completing their work.
STREAMING jobs are continuous jobs that process data streams indefinitely with no natural completion point.
While START, COMPLETE, ABORT, or FAIL events can be emitted, they should not be relied upon as they might occur only occasionally when the streaming job is restarted
The eventCompleteness field in the emission pattern describes what information events contain:
Each event is self-contained for its time period

evidence.text: It states its own status as an open standard for lineage metadata collection: "OpenLineage is an Open Standard for lineage metadata collection designed to record metadata for a job in execution."

evidence.quote: OpenLineage is an Open Standard for lineage metadata collection designed to record metadata for a job in execution.

landscape.text: The options differ on which side of the wire the work is, and the standard is explicit about the problem it removes. Before it: "Each project has to instrument its own custom metadata collection integration, therefore duplicating efforts." After: "Integration efforts are shared across projects." So the value of this card sits on the *producer* side -- the integrations that emit events -- rather than in the choice of backend, which the scope statement makes configurable: "OpenLineage defines the metadata for running jobs and their corresponding events. A configurable backend allows the user to choose what protocol to send the events to." The real tradeoff is therefore not which lineage store to buy. It is how much of a run's meaning a caller is willing to put in custom facets, which are open-ended and unvalidated against anything outside their own schema URL, versus in the three core entities, which are fixed and interoperable. An open vocabulary buys expressiveness and spends the interoperability the standard exists for.

evidence.quote: Each project has to instrument its own custom metadata collection integration, therefore duplicating efforts.
Integration efforts are shared across projects.
OpenLineage defines the metadata for running jobs and their corresponding events. A configurable backend allows the user to choose what protocol to send the events to.

usage.text: A caller at this card does not emit lineage. It declares work; the platform records which run consumed what and produced what, because provenance and the ledger are on the list of things this repo's planning layer decides so the caller does not -- a caller writes an intent and at most one word of profile rather than deciding "decide routing, isolation, retries, model tier, budget ceiling, deadline, telemetry, provenance, the ledger". The consequence for an example built from this card: the assertion is not that the caller emitted a START event, it is that a run which happened is recoverable from the event stream afterwards, with its inputs and outputs named.

gaps.what: `standards` is empty although this card's entire evidence base is one standard. OpenLineage has no directory under standards/, and this repo's rule (docs/reference/cards/BRIEF.md) is that a standards entry names one. The reference model itself carries no standard badge for this card, so the model and the evidence disagree: the model says none, the sources say OpenLineage. It is listed under `tools` as a standard-implementation instead, which is the wrong shelf and is done deliberately rather than silently.
gaps.why_it_matters: Ten of the thirty-four profiles have an empty standards list, so an empty list reads as 'no standard governs this'. Here it means the opposite - a standard governs it and the repo has no folder for it. Those two states should not look identical, and today they do.

gaps.what: A fetch-path fact, recorded because it will recur: github.com/<org>/<repo>/blob/... returns GitHub navigation chrome rather than file text through the gate's fetcher, while raw.githubusercontent.com returns the file. The spec quotes here come from the raw host for that reason, and the raw text carries markdown markers (** and backticks) which are therefore part of the verbatim snippets.
gaps.why_it_matters: bridge.md section 3 warns that capture.py and the gate's fetcher disagree; this is a third case - the same URL returns a document to one host and chrome to another. An agent that reads a blob URL through capture.py, sees the file, and writes the snippet will produce a record the gate cannot verify.
